name: Chinali
confidence_why: Sharma 1991, the only description of Chinali, gives no rule for where word stress falls and is itself unclear whether its monosyllabic pairs (grass/wound, carry/river) show tone or stress, while Sharma 1989 and Chamberlain and Chamberlain 2019 say nothing about stress, so the placement and type of the system remain unknown.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The only primary description does not state where word stress falls. It lists 'tone/stress' among suprasegmentals and illustrates it with two monosyllabic minimal pairs marked with grave/acute diacritics (so no placement information), finds no lexical pitch contrast in isolated words, and separately says that emphatic (utterance-level) stress/pitch goes 'usually' on the initial syllable of the emphasized word. Polysyllabic words in the grammar and vocabulary are transcribed without stress marks.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the 'tone/stress' pairs are monosyllables only (/ghà/ vs /gha/, /né/ vs /ne/).
new_statements.domain_note: Sec. 3.1 concerns isolated (citation-form) monosyllables; sec. 12.2.8 / p.50 concern emphasis within utterances (phrase-level), explicitly 'usually the initial' syllable. Data from two speakers recorded over three days in 1980 (Preface).
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma 1991 describes the speech of the Chahn/Chinal (also 'Sippi', 'Dagi') community of the Pattan valley, Lahul (data from two speakers, 1980) = Glottolog chin1475 / ISO cih. He treats the related Lohari (Lahul Lohar, glottocode laha1254? — sister in Glottolog's 'Chinali-Lahul Lohar' node chin1493) as a separate dialect not covered by this monograph.
